To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the transfer of Cd from cropland fertilizer application to urban areas via insectivorous bats is a new and significant pathway of cross-ecosystems spillover.
the application of fertilizer in rural croplands drives cadmium (Cd)-enrichment in bats dwelling in urban areas, which may pose potential health risks to humans.

the cadmium (Cd), a toxic heavy metal, concentrations in hairs of Chinese Noctule bats, which are urban dwellers, were driven by the fertilizer application intensity (i.e. fertilizer input per unit area) in croplands.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the potential for pollutants in rural croplands, which have been intensively studied, to affect urban areas, which have been less intensively studied, and thus provides an example for the potential for cross-ecosystems spillover of pollutants.
the potential for cross-ecosystems transfer and accumulation of pollutants in urban wildlife, which may have implications for urban ecosystem services and human health.
the potential for Cd accumulation in urban bats that forage on fertilized cropland
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the bats are exposed to Cd from croplands and that this Cd is transferred from the croplands to the urban area via food webs.
the Cd accumulation in the urban Chinese noctule bats was driven by the FAI, which was the most significant factor in the regression model.
the Cd spillover from cropland to urban areas is a significant risk factor for the health of urban wildlife.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Cd spillover from the rural cropland to the urban area through food webs is the main driver of Cd exposure for bats dwelling in an area with a high FAI.
, for the Chinese Noctule bats, their exposure to Cd is driven by regional FAI, and the Cd in their hair can be used to monitor the Cd in croplands.
the bats in this study were not exposed to Cd from urban emissions, but rather from the croplands that the bats forage in.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of chemical fertilizer in rural croplands may drive Cd enrichment in bats dwelling an urban area, and the Cd spillover from the rural to the urban area may have a negative impact on the bats' health.
the use of chemical fertilizers in cropland is the primary driver of Cd accumulation in the bats, which is consistent with the results of previous studies.
the use of fertilizers in rural croplands may drive heavy metal/metalloid contamination in bats that forage in rural areas, but roost in urban areas.
